covers.quote: It is usually more respectful to be specific.
a specific group, use their nation, island or community name
many Aboriginal nations, there may be a regional term that is better, such as ‘Murris’ or ‘Kooris’
many Torres Strait Islander peoples or islands, there may be a regional term that is more appropriate, such as Kulkalgal (encompassing the central islands of Masig, Poruma, Warraber and Iama)
both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, use terms such as ‘First Nations people’, ‘First Australians’ or ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples’.
If you must use it, remember to only do so when writing generally about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

rules.quote: specific terms, like the name of a community, before using broader terms
rules.violation_condition: A reference to a specific First Nations group uses a broad collective label where its nation, island or community name would be more appropriate.
when: For a specific group, use its nation, island or community name.
For multiple Aboriginal nations or Torres Strait Islander communities, a suitable regional term may be more appropriate.
For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples collectively, broad terms such as ‘First Nations people’, ‘First Australians’ or ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples’ are appropriate.
The listed broad terms are examples, not an exhaustive vocabulary.
If ‘Indigenous Australians’ must be used, limit it to general references to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the naming hierarchy and its restatements into one check for the appropriate specificity of a reference.

rules.quote: plurals when speaking about collectives (peoples, nations, cultures, languages)
rules.specification: Distinguish multiple peoples or cultures from multiple individuals. Do not treat the ordinary plural ‘people’ as automatically incorrect or require ‘peoples’ in every reference to individuals.
rules.violation_condition: A reference to multiple distinct First Nations peoples, nations, cultures or languages uses a singular form that presents them as one.
when: Apply when the reference is to more than one people, nation, culture or language.
rules.why: G-2: the listed collective categories are cases of the same singular-versus-plural check.

covers.quote: This use of past tense continues the historical erasure of First Australians.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have always been here. They are still undertaking cultural activities.

examples.note: The surrounding prose explicitly identifies this past-tense usage as erasure.

parts.quote: Many texts have referred to First Nations people in the past tense, for example:
‘The Aboriginal language existed for hundreds of years.’
‘Torres Strait Islanders once congregated at this place.’

examples.note: The lead-in and both list items form one example.

parts.quote: Statements to redress the historical erasure and inaccuracy would read:

‘There is no such thing as “the Aboriginal language”, it would be like saying “the European language”. There are literally hundreds of First Nations languages that exist today, and have been spoken for millennia.’
‘The people of Iama (Yam Island) in the Torres Strait have been living there for thousands of years.’

rules.quote: present tense, unless speaking about a past event
rules.violation_condition: An account of continuing First Nations peoples, languages or cultural activities uses past tense in a way that suggests they no longer exist or continue.
when: Past tense is appropriate when describing a past event.
Do not infer that a continuing language, people or cultural activity has ended merely because its history is being discussed.
rules.why: G-2: keep the past-event exception with the present-tense rule; E-3 keeps each example list together.

covers.quote: empowering, strengths-based language.
deficit language
Content about First Nations people has often focused on ‘problems’. This has 2 outcomes: making First Australians ‘the problem’ or continuing a deficit discourse. Neither is acceptable.
It’s important to acknowledge the many wrongs and ongoing injustices that stem from our shared history. And it's not about ignoring issues.
But it is just as important to acknowledge the strength of those First Australians whose cultures survive and thrive today.

parts.quote: The program supports First Nations people to achieve their goals.
The program seeks to address the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander problems within the community.

rules.quote: Use empowering, strengths-based language.
rules.specification: Assess the framing of people, not whether the subject matter is positive. Describing an injustice or a problem affecting people is not, by itself, deficit language.
rules.violation_condition: Language frames First Nations people themselves as problems or deficits, rather than recognising their agency and strengths.
when: Discussion of wrongs, ongoing injustices and other issues remains appropriate.
Flag deficit framing rather than merely the presence of negative facts.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate repeated strengths-based instructions; G-2 retains the distinction between discussing problems and framing people as problems.

rules.quote: shorthand terms like ‘Aborigines', ‘Islanders’ or acronyms like ‘ATSI’
rules.violation_condition: First Nations people are referred to using shorthand such as ‘Aborigines’, standalone ‘Islanders’ or ‘ATSI’.
when: Apply when these expressions are used to refer to Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people.
The objection to standalone ‘Islanders’ does not prohibit the full term ‘Torres Strait Islanders’.
rules.why: G-2: the listed shorthand forms are cases of one inappropriate-shortening check.

covers.quote: As with any religion or spiritual belief, words like ‘myth’ or ‘legend’ are minimising and hurtful.
A bunyip is a being that many Aboriginal peoples believe is real. Yet many Australians speak of it using terms such as ‘myth’ or ‘legend’.

rules.quote: using terms like ‘myth’, ‘legend’ or ‘folklore’ when referring to the beliefs of First Nations people
rules.violation_condition: First Nations spiritual beliefs or beings are characterised as myths, legends or folklore.
when: Apply when the terms characterise First Nations beliefs, rather than an unrelated use of the same words.
rules.why: G-4: the spirituality section explains and restates the earlier terminology rule rather than creating another finding.

covers.quote: Terms like ‘half-caste’ or ‘part Aboriginal’ reflect these policies. These terms are deeply offensive and hurtful.

rules.quote: blood quantums (for example, ‘half-caste’ or percentage measures)
rules.violation_condition: A person's First Nations identity is described through a blood quantum, fractional ancestry label or percentage measure, including labels such as ‘half-caste’ or ‘part Aboriginal’.
when: Apply to terms used to describe or classify a person's First Nations identity.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: blood fractions, percentages and the later ancestry labels are manifestations of the same check.

covers.quote: ‘us versus them’

rules.quote: Also, setting up a dichotomy of ‘us' and ‘them’ perpetuates division and exclusion. This language use is not acceptable.
rules.violation_condition: Language divides First Nations people and others into opposing ‘us’ and ‘them’ groups in a way that excludes or otherises First Nations people.
when: A pronoun alone is not sufficient: the language must establish the divisive dichotomy described by the rule.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the repeated prohibition; keep othering distinct from deficit framing and paternalism.

covers.quote: ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’, as it also implies ownership, much like ‘our’.

rules.quote: possessive terms such as ‘our’, as in ‘our Aboriginal peoples’
rules.violation_condition: A reference to First Nations peoples implies ownership of them, including ‘our Aboriginal peoples’ or ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’.
when: Assess whether the expression implies ownership of First Nations peoples; do not prohibit every occurrence of a possessive pronoun.
rules.why: G-2: both listed constructions are flagged for the same implication of ownership.

covers.quote: Important cultural practices are also capitalised. For example, Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country.

rules.quote: Always capitalise both.
rules.specification: ‘Both’ refers to Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country. The later capitalisation section extends the convention to important cultural practices; identifying additional practices requires relevant community guidance.
rules.violation_condition: The name ‘Welcome to Country’ or ‘Acknowledgement of Country’, or another important cultural practice covered by the guidance, is written without its required capitals.
when: Apply to names of the cultural practices, not ordinary uses of words such as ‘welcome’.
Where a community has supplied a specific capitalisation preference, assess it under the community-preference rule rather than issuing a second finding.
rules.why: G-4: the later capitalisation passage restates the named-practice requirement; G-2 records community-specific usage as a condition.

covers.quote: In every location in Australia, remote, regional or urban, there are traditional custodians. There may also be many different peoples currently living there.

rules.quote: When writing about any particular place, make sure to be inclusive of all First Nations people living on country.
rules.specification: Interpret inclusion as recognising the First Nations peoples relevant to the account, including both traditional custodians and other First Nations residents. It does not require naming every individual resident.
rules.violation_condition: Content about a place excludes First Nations peoples living there, for example by treating traditional custodians as the only First Nations residents when other peoples also live there.
when: Apply when content describes a particular place and its First Nations peoples.
People living away from their traditional lands must not be excluded merely for that reason.
rules.why: G-2: traditional custodians and other residents are conditions of one inclusion check, not separate rules.

covers.quote: Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear.
Using ‘Indigenous’ alone is inaccurate.

examples.note: Keep the paragraphs together so that the initial full reference establishes the later shortened references.

parts.quote: ‘Indigenous Australians’ is a broad term and covers a large array of peoples. Often Indigenous peoples themselves do not identify using this term, they will use their local community, island or language group.
Indigenous peoples also have regional terms that they use for specific geographical locations, such as ‘palawa’ or ‘Noongar’ to name a couple.

rules.quote: The term should always appear as ‘Indigenous Australians’ in the first instance, always with a capital ‘I’.
rules.violation_condition: The first general reference to First Australians using ‘Indigenous’ omits ‘Australians’, or a later standalone use has no clear Australian referent.
when: Apply when the term is used for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples generally.
After ‘Indigenous Australians’ has established the referent, ‘Indigenous’ may be used if the context remains correct and clear.
The initial-capital requirement is assessed separately.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: first use and permitted contextual shortening form one referent-establishment check; capitalisation is a distinct property.

covers.quote: Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear.
Its use became popular through international discussions, where the term ‘indigenous’ is appropriate (with a lower case ‘i’).

rules.quote: always with a capital ‘I’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Indigenous Australians’, or contextual shorthand ‘Indigenous’ referring to First Australians, is written with a lower-case initial ‘i’.
when: Apply to the Australian collective term and its contextual shorthand.
Lower-case ‘indigenous’ is appropriate in the international context described on the page.
rules.why: G-2: full and shortened Australian terms share one capitalisation check, with international usage as an exception.

covers.quote: The preferred term to describe these languages is ‘sleeping’.

rules.quote: Never refer to them as ‘extinct’.
rules.violation_condition: A First Nations language is described as ‘extinct’.
when: Apply to First Nations languages.
For languages being revived, the preferred description is ‘sleeping’.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the prohibition and preferred replacement address the same lexical choice.

covers.quote: Oral sources must have precedence.

rules.quote: Follow the spellings that local traditional owners, elders or community members use for words from their languages.
rules.violation_condition: A word from a First Nations language is spelt contrary to the relevant community's usage, including where a conflicting written source has been preferred over authoritative oral usage.
when: Establish the relevant local community's spellings rather than assuming that a published spelling is authoritative.
Oral sources take precedence where written sources conflict.
rules.why: G-2: source precedence determines which spelling the same spelling check should accept.

covers.quote: They are Australian languages, not foreign languages.

rules.quote: Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages.
rules.violation_condition: A name or word from a First Nations language is italicised as a foreign-language expression.
when: Apply to names and words from First Nations languages.
rules.why: One typography check; the following sentence explains it rather than adding a rule.

covers.quote: There are few firm rules for capitalisation, as different peoples have their own preferences.
Always ask the relevant community’s preferences and usages, and follow their advice.
Examples of words that are sometimes capitalised include Elders, Country or Traditional Custodians.

rules.quote: But there are many First Australians who have their own preferences, and these should always take precedence.
rules.violation_condition: Capitalisation of a culturally significant term conflicts with the relevant community's stated usage because a default minimal-capitalisation convention has been imposed instead.
when: Apply to capitalisation preferences in the context of this section.
A relevant community's stated preference takes precedence over the page's default minimal capitalisation.
Use this rule for a known community-specific preference rather than also issuing a default-capitalisation finding for the same expression.
rules.why: G-2: community-dependent capitalisation is one conditional check; consultation itself remains writer advice under G-5.

covers.quote: Within some communities, the Dreaming means something very different. It refers to a range of systems of spiritual beliefs.

examples.note: The ordinary English sense is lower case.

parts.quote: For Standard Australian English, ‘dreaming’ has a very particular meaning. For some Aboriginal peoples, there is also another meaning.

examples.note: Only the illustrative sentences are selected, not the sentence stating the capitalisation rule.

parts.quote: Within some communities, the Dreaming means something very different. It refers to a range of systems of spiritual beliefs.

rules.quote: It should always be capitalised when used in this way.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Dreaming’ is written with a lower-case initial when it denotes the Aboriginal systems of spiritual beliefs described in the passage.
when: Apply to the spiritual sense of ‘Dreaming’, not ordinary Standard Australian English ‘dreaming’.
Where a relevant community has supplied a specific capitalisation preference, assess that preference instead of issuing a duplicate default-capitalisation finding.
rules.why: G-4: the operative rule is prose beneath an Example label; its meaning-dependent capitalisation must not be missed.

rules.quote: Tell positive stories.
rules.specification: The page does not specify how much positive storytelling is required or whether short factual content is exempt. Do not invent a numerical quota.
rules.violation_condition: Content about First Nations people contains no positive stories or accounts of their strengths and achievements.
when: Apply to content about First Nations people.
Positive storytelling does not require ignoring wrongs, ongoing injustices or other issues.
rules.why: This concerns the presence of positive accounts across content, distinct from deficit wording in an individual sentence; leave the unstated threshold unresolved.

rules.quote: Emphasise ongoing connections to community, culture and country.
rules.specification: The page gives no threshold for sufficient emphasis or guidance about which short or specialised texts must discuss these connections.
rules.violation_condition: Content about First Nations people omits or obscures their continuing connections to community, culture and country.
when: Apply to content about First Nations people and their cultures or communities.
Assess continuing connections across the content, not by requiring a fixed phrase in every sentence.
rules.why: The missing recognition of continuing connections is distinct from tense errors or deficit wording; no emphasis threshold is supplied.

covers.quote: They are not ‘in need’ of being ‘rescued’ or ‘saved’.
It is about working together, not doing things ‘for them’ or ‘to them’.

rules.quote: Be careful not to perpetuate patronising or paternalistic language use.
rules.violation_condition: Language portrays First Nations people as dependent recipients needing others to rescue, save or act for them, rather than as people with agency.
when: Assess the framing rather than automatically flagging every occurrence of ‘for them’, ‘saved’ or similar words.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: rescue framing and doing things to or for people illustrate one paternalism check.

rules.quote: Communicate clearly without jargon or acronyms.
rules.violation_condition: Written communication used in consultation with a First Nations community contains jargon or acronyms.
when: Apply to written cross-cultural communication in the consultation context described here.
Other consultation actions, such as listening and allowing time, are not properties of the text.
rules.why: G-5: unlike the surrounding process advice, jargon and acronyms are observable properties of written communication.

covers.quote: There might be some avoidance protocols you need to adhere to.

Some communities are okay these days with the use of a name, an image, or both. Others still request the use of neither. The community will have a way to refer to someone in this case and can give guidance.
Using a standard warning does not replace respectful consultation with the community.

rules.quote: Always adhere to these requirements for all community members.
rules.violation_condition: Text uses a deceased community member's name contrary to applicable family or community avoidance requirements, or fails to use the prescribed alternative reference.
when: Apply when a person has died and the relevant family or community has specified naming requirements.
Some communities permit names; others require an alternative reference.
A standard warning about deceased people does not waive the community's requirements.
This text check concerns names and textual references, not image selection.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: community-specific restrictions and permissions govern one naming check; obtaining approval is a separate writer process under G-5.

anchor.quote: specific terms, like the name of a community, before using broader terms

covers.prefix: d or how they want to identify.
covers.quote: It is usually more respectful to be specific.
a specific group, use their nation, island or community name
many Aboriginal nations, there may be a regional term that is better, such as ‘Murris’ or ‘Kooris’
many Torres Strait Islander peoples or islands, there may be a regional term that is more appropriate, such as Kulkalgal (encompassing the central islands of Masig, Poruma, Warraber and Iama)
both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, use terms such as ‘First Nations people’, ‘First Australians’ or ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples’.
If you must use it, remember to only do so when writing generally about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
covers.suffix: The term should always appear a

tags.violation_condition: A reference to a specific First Nations group uses a broad collective label where its nation, island or community name would be more appropriate.

when: For a specific group, use its nation, island or community name.
For multiple Aboriginal nations or Torres Strait Islander communities, a suitable regional term may be more appropriate.
For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples collectively, broad terms such as ‘First Nations people’, ‘First Australians’ or ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples’ are appropriate.
The listed broad terms are examples, not an exhaustive vocabulary.
If ‘Indigenous Australians’ must be used, limit it to general references to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the naming hierarchy and its restatements into one check for the appropriate specificity of a reference.

anchor.quote: plurals when speaking about collectives (peoples, nations, cultures, languages)

tags.specification: Distinguish multiple peoples or cultures from multiple individuals. Do not treat the ordinary plural ‘people’ as automatically incorrect or require ‘peoples’ in every reference to individuals.
tags.violation_condition: A reference to multiple distinct First Nations peoples, nations, cultures or languages uses a singular form that presents them as one.

when: Apply when the reference is to more than one people, nation, culture or language.
rules.why: G-2: the listed collective categories are cases of the same singular-versus-plural check.

anchor.quote: present tense, unless speaking about a past event

covers.quote: This use of past tense continues the historical erasure of First Australians.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have always been here. They are still undertaking cultural activities.
covers.suffix: Be conscious of this and work t

examples.note: The surrounding prose explicitly identifies this past-tense usage as erasure.

parts.quote: Many texts have referred to First Nations people in the past tense, for example:
‘The Aboriginal language existed for hundreds of years.’
‘Torres Strait Islanders once congregated at this place.’

examples.note: The lead-in and both list items form one example.

parts.quote: Statements to redress the historical erasure and inaccuracy would read:

‘There is no such thing as “the Aboriginal language”, it would be like saying “the European language”. There are literally hundreds of First Nations languages that exist today, and have been spoken for millennia.’
‘The people of Iama (Yam Island) in the Torres Strait have been living there for thousands of years.’

tags.violation_condition: An account of continuing First Nations peoples, languages or cultural activities uses past tense in a way that suggests they no longer exist or continue.

when: Past tense is appropriate when describing a past event.
Do not infer that a continuing language, people or cultural activity has ended merely because its history is being discussed.
rules.why: G-2: keep the past-event exception with the present-tense rule; E-3 keeps each example list together.

anchor.quote: Use empowering, strengths-based language.

covers.quote: empowering, strengths-based language.
deficit language
Content about First Nations people has often focused on ‘problems’. This has 2 outcomes: making First Australians ‘the problem’ or continuing a deficit discourse. Neither is acceptable.
It’s important to acknowledge the many wrongs and ongoing injustices that stem from our shared history. And it's not about ignoring issues.
covers.suffix: But it is just as important to

covers.quote: But it is just as important to acknowledge the strength of those First Australians whose cultures survive and thrive today.

parts.quote: The program supports First Nations people to achieve their goals.
The program seeks to address the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander problems within the community.

tags.specification: Assess the framing of people, not whether the subject matter is positive. Describing an injustice or a problem affecting people is not, by itself, deficit language.
tags.violation_condition: Language frames First Nations people themselves as problems or deficits, rather than recognising their agency and strengths.

when: Discussion of wrongs, ongoing injustices and other issues remains appropriate.
Flag deficit framing rather than merely the presence of negative facts.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate repeated strengths-based instructions; G-2 retains the distinction between discussing problems and framing people as problems.

anchor.quote: shorthand terms like ‘Aborigines', ‘Islanders’ or acronyms like ‘ATSI’

tags.violation_condition: First Nations people are referred to using shorthand such as ‘Aborigines’, standalone ‘Islanders’ or ‘ATSI’.

when: Apply when these expressions are used to refer to Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people.
The objection to standalone ‘Islanders’ does not prohibit the full term ‘Torres Strait Islanders’.
rules.why: G-2: the listed shorthand forms are cases of one inappropriate-shortening check.

anchor.quote: using terms like ‘myth’, ‘legend’ or ‘folklore’ when referring to the beliefs of First Nations people

covers.prefix: at is only now being addressed.
covers.quote: As with any religion or spiritual belief, words like ‘myth’ or ‘legend’ are minimising and hurtful.
A bunyip is a being that many Aboriginal peoples believe is real. Yet many Australians speak of it using terms such as ‘myth’ or ‘legend’.
covers.suffix: They also use it without permis

tags.violation_condition: First Nations spiritual beliefs or beings are characterised as myths, legends or folklore.

when: Apply when the terms characterise First Nations beliefs, rather than an unrelated use of the same words.
rules.why: G-4: the spirituality section explains and restates the earlier terminology rule rather than creating another finding.

anchor.quote: blood quantums (for example, ‘half-caste’ or percentage measures)

covers.prefix: rry, and where they could live.
covers.quote: Terms like ‘half-caste’ or ‘part Aboriginal’ reflect these policies. These terms are deeply offensive and hurtful.

tags.violation_condition: A person's First Nations identity is described through a blood quantum, fractional ancestry label or percentage measure, including labels such as ‘half-caste’ or ‘part Aboriginal’.

when: Apply to terms used to describe or classify a person's First Nations identity.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: blood fractions, percentages and the later ancestry labels are manifestations of the same check.

anchor.quote: Also, setting up a dichotomy of ‘us' and ‘them’ perpetuates division and exclusion. This language use is not acceptable.

covers.quote: ‘us versus them’

tags.violation_condition: Language divides First Nations people and others into opposing ‘us’ and ‘them’ groups in a way that excludes or otherises First Nations people.

when: A pronoun alone is not sufficient: the language must establish the divisive dichotomy described by the rule.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate the repeated prohibition; keep othering distinct from deficit framing and paternalism.

anchor.quote: possessive terms such as ‘our’, as in ‘our Aboriginal peoples’

covers.quote: ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’, as it also implies ownership, much like ‘our’.

tags.violation_condition: A reference to First Nations peoples implies ownership of them, including ‘our Aboriginal peoples’ or ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’.

when: Assess whether the expression implies ownership of First Nations peoples; do not prohibit every occurrence of a possessive pronoun.
rules.why: G-2: both listed constructions are flagged for the same implication of ownership.

anchor.quote: Always capitalise both.

covers.quote: Important cultural practices are also capitalised. For example, Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country.

tags.specification: ‘Both’ refers to Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country. The later capitalisation section extends the convention to important cultural practices; identifying additional practices requires relevant community guidance.
tags.violation_condition: The name ‘Welcome to Country’ or ‘Acknowledgement of Country’, or another important cultural practice covered by the guidance, is written without its required capitals.

when: Apply to names of the cultural practices, not ordinary uses of words such as ‘welcome’.
Where a community has supplied a specific capitalisation preference, assess it under the community-preference rule rather than issuing a second finding.
rules.why: G-4: the later capitalisation passage restates the named-practice requirement; G-2 records community-specific usage as a condition.

anchor.quote: When writing about any particular place, make sure to be inclusive of all First Nations people living on country.

covers.quote: In every location in Australia, remote, regional or urban, there are traditional custodians. There may also be many different peoples currently living there.

tags.specification: Interpret inclusion as recognising the First Nations peoples relevant to the account, including both traditional custodians and other First Nations residents. It does not require naming every individual resident.
tags.violation_condition: Content about a place excludes First Nations peoples living there, for example by treating traditional custodians as the only First Nations residents when other peoples also live there.

when: Apply when content describes a particular place and its First Nations peoples.
People living away from their traditional lands must not be excluded merely for that reason.
rules.why: G-2: traditional custodians and other residents are conditions of one inclusion check, not separate rules.

anchor.quote: The term should always appear as ‘Indigenous Australians’ in the first instance, always with a capital ‘I’.

covers.quote: Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear.

covers.prefix: e context is correct and clear.
covers.quote: Using ‘Indigenous’ alone is inaccurate.

examples.note: Keep the paragraphs together so that the initial full reference establishes the later shortened references.

parts.quote: ‘Indigenous Australians’ is a broad term and covers a large array of peoples. Often Indigenous peoples themselves do not identify using this term, they will use their local community, island or language group.
Indigenous peoples also have regional terms that they use for specific geographical locations, such as ‘palawa’ or ‘Noongar’ to name a couple.

tags.violation_condition: The first general reference to First Australians using ‘Indigenous’ omits ‘Australians’, or a later standalone use has no clear Australian referent.

when: Apply when the term is used for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples generally.
After ‘Indigenous Australians’ has established the referent, ‘Indigenous’ may be used if the context remains correct and clear.
The initial-capital requirement is assessed separately.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: first use and permitted contextual shortening form one referent-establishment check; capitalisation is a distinct property.

anchor.quote: always with a capital ‘I’.

covers.quote: Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear.

rules.why: G-2: full and shortened Australian terms share one capitalisation check, with international usage as an exception.
